doc.title: Marty Grosz interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995

title: Mother's 'swing orchestras' quote; first ukulele and no piano at home
summary: Rowe asks about the quote on the CD title. Grosz recalls his mother, the school ukulele and his father's possible disdain for a bourgeois piano.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: We are filming today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive, attending the L.A. Classic Jazz Fest and it’s our pleasure to have with us Marty Grosz, who is an acoustic guitarist and purveyor of a special form of jazz I think, that we’re going to try to get a handle on here. Thanks for your time in joining us today. I have to, I want to start out and ask you, and you have to excuse my accent, okay, but what is this statement here, “Do you mean you vant to sit in vront of dose schving orchestras un do ching, ching, ching all night?”

Yes, that was my mother, who was very happy. I had sort of learned secretly, because I don’t know, you know when you really care about something, I really cared. I’m not one of those guys who had an instrument thrust in his hand although I did have a ukulele thrust in my hand when I was about eight years old. We had lessons at school but it didn’t work, all of us sat around, twenty kids in one room, people banging on drums, pianos, all that stuff, trombones, and what are you going to do with a uke? Nothing. You know, that’s the only instrument we had at home. I think my father, my mother actually wanted to have a piano, but we were in a rented house and I think my father, I don’t know if this is true, but he might have thought that the piano was too much of a symbol of some kind of bourgeois respectability.
And we wouldn’t want that, right?

I’m assuming that. So I think that on the scale of things important to spend money on at a time when money was not that available, I think he probably would have thought you know, he remembered from his youth in Germany, every house had what they called the “gout de stoupa,” the good room that was like the living room that was never used. You know what I mean? And the piano was often this sacred symbol with a piano scarf on it, and don’t put this on it, don’t put that, don’t touch that, that’s the piano.
